stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
stimulus:
The following text is from Ruth Okafor's 1998 memoir about her years as a vaccination nurse.

Every morning before dawn I packed the clinic cooler: vials of measles vaccine, boxes of syringes, ice packs wrapped in newspaper. When spring rains washed out the road to the hill villages, I walked the last mile with the cooler strapped to my back. <u>It always weighed more than anything inside it, because every name on my list was a child waiting at the end of that road.</u>
choices: It explains that the cooler was built of heavy materials that made it hard to carry.
It conveys the sense of responsibility the narrator felt toward the children she served.
It describes the narrator's conversations with families about the vaccination schedule.
It suggests that the narrator resented having to walk the last mile to the villages.
explanation: The underlined sentence says the cooler 'weighed more than anything inside it' and gives the reason: each name on the list was 'a child waiting.' That extra weight is figurative. It is the weight of knowing that children depend on her. So the sentence shows her sense of responsibility.

A.why: You read the image literally. The text never describes what the cooler is made of. The 'because' clause tells you the weight comes from the children waiting, not from the cooler's materials.

C.why: You added a scene the text doesn't contain. The narrator mentions a list of names but never says she talked with any family. Before you pick a choice, check that you can point to the words that support it.

D.why: You misread the tone. The sentence explains why the load felt heavy: children were waiting for her. That shows devotion, not resentment. Nothing in the text suggests she minded the walk.

stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
stimulus:
The following text is from Lucía Ferrante's 2011 novel The Dry Field. Teodora has returned to her family's farm after a year at an agricultural research station.

Her father judged a field the way his own father had: he crumbled a handful of soil between his fingers, smelled it, and announced whether it was ready. <u>Teodora pushed a steel probe into the same ground and read the nitrogen level off a screen to the second decimal place.</u> Neither of them, she suspected, was entirely wrong.
choices: It explains the scientific process by which the probe measures nitrogen in soil.
It shows that Teodora considers her father's method of judging soil useless.
It contrasts Teodora's way of assessing the field with her father's way.
It describes an argument Teodora and her father had about whether to plant.
explanation: The sentence before the underlined one shows the father testing soil by touch and smell. The underlined sentence shows Teodora testing 'the same ground' with a probe and a screen. Putting the two methods side by side sets up a contrast between the characters, and the last sentence comments on that contrast.

A.why: You focused on the probe and missed the sentence's job. The text names the tool and its reading but never explains how it works. The sentence is there to set Teodora's method against her father's.

B.why: You missed the final sentence. Teodora suspects 'neither of them' is 'entirely wrong,' so she does not think her father's method is useless.

D.why: You invented a conversation. The text describes two ways of testing soil and one private thought of Teodora's. Nobody argues, and nothing is said about planting.

stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
stimulus:
The following text is from Harold Visser's 1987 short story "The Inspector."

For thirty years Marguerite had climbed beneath the river bridge with a flashlight and a small hammer. She tapped each rivet and listened for the dull note that meant rust. She recorded every hairline crack in a green notebook, and she knew which ones had widened since the winter before. <u>The bridge, in other words, had been the one long conversation of her life.</u>
choices: It sums up the earlier details by casting Marguerite's work as a lifelong relationship.
It reveals that Marguerite spoke aloud to the bridge while she inspected it.
It describes a repair Marguerite made after she discovered rust on a rivet.
It suggests that Marguerite found her years of inspections dull and repetitive.
explanation: 'In other words' tells you the sentence restates what came before it. Thirty years of tapping, listening, and tracking cracks are recast as a 'conversation,' which is a figure for a close, two-way relationship. The sentence summarizes the details and tells you what they meant to her.

B.why: You took 'conversation' literally. The tapping and listening are what make the image fit. The text never says Marguerite talked to the bridge.

C.why: You added an event. The passage covers inspecting and recording only: tapping, listening, and writing in a notebook. No repair is ever mentioned.

D.why: You probably caught the word 'dull,' but in the text it describes the sound that means rust, not her feelings. Calling the bridge 'the one long conversation of her life' shows close attachment, not boredom.

stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
stimulus:
The following text is from Asha Lindqvist's 2004 novel The Breaking Point.

Over the past year, Dr. Imani Reyes had loaded four hundred ceramic samples into the press. Each one held its shape for a moment under the load and then burst into white dust. <u>The four hundred and first held.</u> Reyes stood very still, as if moving might undo it.
choices: It explains why the earlier ceramic samples burst apart under the press.
It describes how Reyes gripped the final sample to keep it in the press.
It shows that Reyes had lost interest in her long series of experiments.
It marks the moment when Reyes's long string of failed tests finally ends.
explanation: The sentence before it describes four hundred samples that all burst. The underlined sentence reports that the next one 'held,' meaning it survived the press. The sentence after it shows Reyes frozen in place, almost afraid to believe it. The underlined line is the turning point that ends the run of failures.

A.why: You assigned the sentence a job it doesn't do. The text says the earlier samples burst but never says why. The underlined sentence is about the one sample that didn't.

B.why: You read 'held' as gripping something with a hand. The previous sentence uses 'held its shape,' which tells you 'held' here means the sample survived the load. Nobody holds anything.

C.why: You missed her reaction. Reyes stands 'very still, as if moving might undo it,' which shows intense investment in the result, not a lack of interest.

stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
stimulus:
The following text is from Nadia Okonkwo-Bell's 2015 memoir about her training as a folklorist.

When I began recording my grandmother's stories, I arrived with a new microphone and a typed list of questions. She set the list aside without reading it. Then she told the tale of the fox who borrowed the moon, which I had heard a hundred times at her kitchen table. <u>Somewhere in the telling, I stopped being a researcher and became her granddaughter again.</u>
choices: It summarizes the plot of the tale about the fox who borrowed the moon.
It shows the narrator shifting from a professional role to a personal one.
It reveals that the grandmother had long disliked researchers from the university.
It suggests that the narrator was hearing the fox tale for the first time.
explanation: The narrator arrives with a microphone and a question list, which are the tools of a researcher. As her grandmother tells a familiar tale, the underlined sentence says she 'stopped being a researcher and became her granddaughter again.' Its job is to mark that change from a professional role to a family one.

A.why: You fixed on the fox tale, which is only background. The text gives the tale's title and never its plot. The underlined sentence is about the narrator, not the story.

C.why: You invented a dislike. The grandmother sets the list aside, but the text never says how she feels about researchers or mentions a university. Make sure you can point to the words that support a choice.

D.why: The text says the narrator had heard the tale 'a hundred times at her kitchen table.' That familiarity is part of why she feels like a granddaughter again.

stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
stimulus:
The following text is from Emil Sørhaug's 1979 novel The Long Winter Sky.

The night Halvard first looked at Saturn through the observatory's great refractor, he stepped back from the eyepiece twice, half sure the rings had been painted on the glass. <u>He felt as though someone had handed him a secret too large to carry.</u> On the long walk home he said nothing at all.
choices: It conveys the overwhelming sense of wonder Halvard felt at what he had seen.
It indicates that an astronomer gave Halvard a written account of Saturn's rings.
It suggests that Halvard was disappointed by how small Saturn appeared.
It explains why Halvard's companion refused to speak on the walk home.
explanation: Halvard can hardly believe what he sees, so he steps back twice. Afterward he says nothing all the way home. Between these two details, the underlined sentence compares the experience to being given 'a secret too large to carry.' It tells you how he feels: overwhelmed and amazed.

B.why: You read the comparison literally. 'As though' tells you nobody actually handed him anything. The 'secret' is a figure for what he saw through the telescope.

C.why: You reversed his reaction. Thinking the rings might be painted on the glass, and falling silent afterward, show amazement, not disappointment. The text never mentions Saturn's size.

D.why: You invented a character. It is Halvard who says nothing on the walk home, and the text never mentions a companion.

stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
stimulus:
The following text is from Daniel Achterberg's 2008 memoir of his career with a state water survey.

As a boy, I believed the river was always the same river: brown, slow, and older than the town itself. Then I took a job measuring its flow, and I learned otherwise. <u>Some mornings the gauge read double what it had a week earlier, and the water passing my boots had fallen as snow on mountains I had never seen.</u>
choices: It explains the method the state survey used to measure the river's flow.
It shows that the narrator came to regret taking the job with the survey.
It describes the narrator's trip to the distant mountains where the snow fell.
It illustrates how the narrator's childhood view of the river proved mistaken.
explanation: The text opens with an old belief: the river was 'always the same river.' Then the narrator says 'I learned otherwise.' The underlined sentence gives the evidence. The flow doubles in a week, and the water comes from distant snow. Its job is to show that the river changes constantly, which corrects what he believed as a boy.

A.why: You chose a choice that describes what the sentence mentions, a gauge reading, rather than what the sentence does. The text never explains how the measuring works. The reading is there to show that the river changes.

B.why: You added a feeling the text never shows. The narrator says the job taught him something, and nothing suggests he was sorry he took it.

C.why: The sentence says the snow fell on 'mountains I had never seen,' so the narrator never went there.

stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
stimulus:
The following text is from Rosa Delacroix-Tan's 2019 novel Splits.

All summer Marisol ran on a treadmill in the university's performance lab, wires taped to her chest and a mask over her mouth that measured every breath. The researchers called her their model subject. <u>On the first day of the cross-country season, she peeled the tape from her skin and ran into the woods without looking back.</u>
choices: It shows that Marisol preferred the treadmill to running outdoors.
It indicates that the tape on Marisol's chest had injured her skin.
It conveys Marisol's eagerness to leave the confines of the lab behind.
It describes Marisol quitting the study after an argument with the researchers.
explanation: The first sentences show Marisol wired, masked, and measured all summer. In the underlined sentence she peels off the tape and runs into the woods 'without looking back.' Set against the lab scene, that action shows how eager she is to get free of it.

A.why: You reversed what her action shows. She runs into the woods 'without looking back,' which suggests she is glad to leave the treadmill, not that she prefers it.

B.why: You read a physical detail too literally and added to it. Peeling off tape is a gesture of breaking free. The text never mentions an injury.

D.why: You invented a scene. The text has no argument and never says she quit the study. The only thing the researchers say is that she is their 'model subject.'
